*Svapnavāsavadattam*
[After the benediction, the Stage Manager enters. Stage Manager:
O you who possess the strength of Vāsavadattā, whose complexion is like the moon of Udayana—[I bow] to you!
May the two arms, reddish-brown like Vasantaka and full from having descended into Padmāvatī, protect [us].
Thus I inform the noble ones:
"Ah! While I am intent on making this announcement, what indeed is this sound that is heard? Come, let me look."
[Offstage] Move aside, move aside, noble sirs! Move aside!
*Sūtradhāra*: Very well, I understand.
By the affectionate servants of the King of Magadha who followed the princess,
all the people dwelling in the penance grove were boldly driven away.
{Having exited} [stage direction];
{having entered}.
*{Guards}—Move aside, move aside, sirs! Move aside!* [Move aside, move aside, noble ones!
*{Then enters Yaugandharāyaṇa in the guise of a wandering mendicant, and Vāsavadattā wearing the dress of a woman from Avanti.}*
*{Yaugandharāyaṇa}:* — {Listening} What? Is he being driven away even here?
From where?

A sense of alarm is aroused in this wise man—who dwells in a hermitage, content with wild fruits, clad in bark garments, and worthy of honor—by a man intoxicated with fortune, devoid of discipline, and filled with pride: "Who is this that, by his command, turns this tranquil grove of asceticism into a mere village? (BhSv 1.3)
Vāsavadattā: Noble sir, who is this that drives me away? Yaugandharāyaṇa: Madam, it is he who drives himself away from the Dharma.
Vāsavadattā: Noble sir, it was not my intention to speak thus; indeed, I did not think that I too would have to be set aside.
Yaugandharāyaṇa: Lady, when deities are unrecognized, they are treated with contempt.
Vāsavadattā: Noble sir, physical exhaustion does not produce such distress as this humiliation does.
Yaugandharāyaṇa: This realm has been cast off by her highness like food that has already been eaten and discarded.
No concern should be felt here;
for previously you too went thus as desired, and you shall go again in praise through victory over your master.
In the course of time, the sequence of fortune for the world proceeds like a row of wheel-spokes revolving.
*{The two servants}:—Move aside, sirs, move aside! (BhSv_1.4:1) [Move away, noble ones, move away!
{Then enters the chamberlain.} (BhSv_1.4:2)
Chamberlain: Sambhāṣaka, indeed, indeed no one is to be cleared away! Behold: may you avoid bringing reproach upon the king; harshness should not be employed toward those dwelling in the hermitage.
In order to escape the contempt of the city, these wise men have gone to the forest and dwell there.
*{Both}:— Noble sir, so be it.
(They both exit.)*
Yaugandharāyaṇa: Ah! His insight is truly perceptive. My child, let us approach him for now.
Vāsavadattā: Noble sir, so be it.
[Noble sir, it is so.
Yaugandharāyaṇa— [approaching]— O sir, for what purpose is this clearing away?
Chamberlain: O ascetic!
Yaugandharāyaṇa:
(To himself) "Ascetic"—this is indeed an address befitting one of merit.
"But because of my lack of acquaintance, it does not take root in my mind.
*Chamberlain:* "Sir, please listen.
This is indeed Padmāvatī by name, the sister of our Great King Darśaka, whose name was bestowed upon him by his elders."
This very woman, having approached our mother, the Great Queen, while she is staying in the hermitage, will depart for Rājagṛha with her permission;
therefore, she intends to dwell in this hermitage today.
Therefore, sirs...
"Let the ascetics freely bring water from the sacred fords, sacrificial fuel, flowers, and *darbha* grass from the forest;
for the princess, who loves righteousness, would never wish to cause distress to those practicing dharma, as this is her family vow toward ascetics."
*{Yaugandharāyaṇa}:*—
*(To himself)* This is she, the daughter of the King of Magadha named Padmāvatī, who was prophesied by Puṣpaka-bhadra and others as the one who would become the queen of my lord.
From that conceptualization, either aversion or great esteem arises;
because of my longing for the wife of my master, I have a great sense of ownership toward her.
Vāsavadattā—
(To herself) Hearing that she is a princess, a feeling of sisterly affection for her arises within me as well.
Then enters Padmāvatī with her retinue and a maidservant.
The maidservant says: "Come, come, my lady;
please enter this hermitage."
"Let the princess come; let her enter this hermitage.
Then enters a seated female ascetic.
Ascetic: "Welcome to the princess!"
"Welcome to the princess!
*Vāsavadattā*— (to herself)— this is that very princess.
"Indeed, her form is worthy of her noble lineage.
(This is that princess;
truly, her beauty is commensurate with her high birth.)"
Padmāvatī: Noble lady, I pay homage to you. Ascetic woman: May you live long.
Enter, child, enter! Indeed, these penance groves are like one's own home to a guest.
Live long! Enter, child, enter!
"The penance groves are, as it were, one's own home for a guest.
Padmāvatī: "Be that so, be that so! Noble lady, I am at ease."
I am favored by these words of great respect.
(BhSv_1.7:15) [Let it be, let it be!
Noble lady, I am reassured.]
"I have been favored by these words of great respect.
Vāsavadattā—(to herself)—"Indeed, it is not only her beauty; her speech too is truly sweet."

[“Indeed, it is not only her beauty; her speech too is sweet. The Female Ascetic: “My lady, does no king at all seek the hand of this sister of Bhadramukha? (BhSv_1.7:17) [“My lady, does no king at all seek the hand of this sister of Bhadramukha?”]
Maid:
There is a king named Pradyota in Ujjayinī; he is sending an envoy for the sake of the girl.
He sends a messenger on account of the boy.
Vāsavadattā—
(to herself)— Let it be, let it be!
"Now she has become her own mistress.
(Let it be, let it be;
now she has indeed become her own.)
Ascetic: This appearance is indeed worthy of such great respect;
it is heard that both royal families are of high status.
"It is heard that both royal families are most eminent.
Padmāvatī said: "Noble sir, has the sage been seen?
Let the ascetic folk be invited to bestow their favor by granting what they desire; let it be asked first, 'Who wishes for what here?'"
"Noble one, has the community of sages been seen?
Let the ascetics be invited to grant their desired gifts; let it be asked who desires what here.
The Chamberlain replied: "Whatever it is that you desire."
"O you ascetics dwelling in the hermitage,
listen, all of you, listen!
Here, this lady, the daughter of the King of Magadha, having developed confidence through this trust, invites me for the sake of the Dharma."
For whose sake is this water-pot? Who seeks clothing as if it were already determined? Having completed the initiation, what does he desire? What might still need to be given to the teacher?
Here, the daughter of the king, who is fond of the joy of Dharma, desires favor for herself. Let each person say whatever they wish for; tell me now, what should be given to whom?
*Yaugandharāyaṇa*: Ah, an expedient has been found!
[Aloud] O sir, I am a seeker!
*Padmāvatī*: By good fortune, my visit to the penance grove has been successful!
[“By good fortune, my journey to the penance grove has borne fruit! The Female Ascetic: This hermitage must have been visited by someone who brings satisfaction to the ascetics.
"This hermitage is inhabited by contented ascetics; this must be some newcomer.
The Chamberlain: "O sir, what shall be done?"

Yaugandharāyaṇa: This is my sister; I desire that her ladyship should protect this woman, whose husband is away, for some time. Why? [Because: *{yaugandharāyaṇaḥ}* — this is my sister (BhSv_1.8:7); I wish for her, who is separated from her husband, to be protected by your honor for a certain period (BhSv_1.8:8).
From where [is this known]?
"I have not donned this saffron robe for the sake of wealth, nor for enjoyments, nor for garments;
rather, this wise maiden, who has observed the practice of the Dharma, is capable of protecting my sister's conduct."
Vāsavadattā—
(to herself) Ah!
Here is my noble master Yaugandharāyaṇa wishing to entrust me to him.
Let it be; let him do as he pleases without hesitation.
(BhSv_1.9:3) [I am here; the noble Yaugandharāyaṇa wishes to entrust me to him. Very well.]
[He] will not act without having considered the sequence.
*Chamberlain*: "Your Majesty, his reliance [on you] is indeed great;
how shall we give our consent?"
Whence could there be happiness? Wealth would be for the sake of giving; life is happiness, and austerity is happiness;
everything else may be happiness, but the guarding of what has been entrusted is suffering.
Padmāvatī: Noble sir, having first proclaimed "Who desires what?", it is improper to deliberate now; let the noble sir do exactly as he says.
"Let the noble one carry out what he says.
Chamberlain: This which you have said is appropriate, lady. Maid: May the princess live long, she who speaks such truth!
[“May the lady, who speaks thus truthfully, live long!
The Female Ascetic: “May you live long, blessed one!
May you live long!”
Chamberlain:
My lady, having approached [her],
has the protection of her venerable sister been accepted by your venerable self?
Yaugandharāyaṇa: I am favored by your ladyship.
Child, approach her ladyship Vāsavadattā.
Vāsavadattā: [Approaches.]
[To herself: What recourse is there? I, unfortunate as I am, must go this way.
Padmāvatī: Let it be, let it be; she has now become my own.
[She has now become my own.
The female ascetic: "Given her appearance, I suspect that she too is a princess."
Maid: The noble lady speaks well; I too perceive that I have experienced happiness.
"I too see that I have experienced happiness.
[Yaugandharāyaṇa]—[to himself]—"Ah! Half of the burden has now been laid down."
Just as it has been deliberated upon with the ministers, so shall it turn out.
Therefore, once the master is established, this lady here—the daughter of the King of Magadha—will serve as a source of confidence for me as I lead the venerable lady [to him].
Why?

Padmāvatī shall become the queen of the king; for those by whom misfortune was first foreseen, this has been done because of their conviction, for destiny does not bypass well-examined words of the perfected ones.
Then enters a religious student (*brahmacārī*). [The religious student],
looking upward:
"It is midday;
I am utterly exhausted.
Now, in what place shall I rest?"
(Walking about: Well, I have seen it;
there must be a penance grove nearby.
For thus it is:
deer roam with confidence, unafraid, certain that no danger has come to this place; all the trees, their branches rich with flowers and fruit, are protected by compassion;
the herds of cows, mostly tawny, abound as the wealth of the land; the quarters of the sky are not barren; and this smoke, resting upon many sources, leaves no doubt that this is a grove of ascetics.
I shall enter. (Having entered) Ah! This person is indeed contrary to the nature of a hermitage.
(Looking elsewhere) Or rather, ascetics may also be found here.
"An approach that is free from fault.
"O, a woman!
*Chamberlain:* "Please enter at your leisure, sir."
The hermitage named Sarvajanasādhāraṇa.
Vāsavadattā: Ah!
Padmāvatī: Oh, my lady avoids the sight of other men.
"Ah!
The noble lady avoids the sight of other men.
Well then, this trust must indeed be well-guarded."
Chamberlain: O sir, we have already entered;
please accept this hospitality due to a guest. Student:
{Having sipped water} Let it be, let it be;
I am now relieved of my fatigue.
{Yaugandharāyaṇa}—O sir, from where have you come?
Where should one go?
Where is the noble one’s abode? "O celibate practitioner, listen! "Sir, please listen."
From Rājagṛha, for the sake of furthering my learning, I went to the land of Vatsa; there, in a village named Lāvāṇaka, I resided.
— Vāsavadattā —
[To herself] Alas, Lāvāṇaka!
At the mere mention of Lāvāṇaka, my fever seems to be renewed once again.
[My] grief has been renewed, as it were, by the mention of Lāvāṇaka.
*Yaugandharāyaṇa*: Now, the science is completed.
*The Vedic Student*: Indeed, not yet.
Yaugandharāyaṇa: If your learning is not yet complete, what is the purpose of your arrival?
Brahmacārī: A truly terrible calamity has occurred there.
Yaugandharāyaṇa: How so?
"Brahmacārī": There dwells a king named Udayana.
"Yaugandharāyaṇa": It is heard that the venerable Udayana is there. "Is he? [he asked].
*{Brahmacārī}: It is said that his wife, named Vāsavadattā, the daughter of the King of Avanti, was dearly beloved by him.
*{Yaugandharāyaṇa}: It must have been so;
what happened after that?
*Brahmacārī*: Then, while that king had gone out on a hunt, she was burned by a village fire.
*Vāsavadattā* (to herself):
This is false, this is indeed false!
I live, unfortunate as I am!
(This is indeed a lie, a lie;
I live, unfortunate as I am!)
*Yaugandharāyaṇa*: And then what happened?
*Brahmacārī*: Then the minister named Yaugandharāyaṇa, desiring to rescue her, threw himself into that very fire.
*Yaugandharāyaṇa*: It is true, he has fallen.
"Then what happened?

"The religious student replied: 'After he had returned, the king, having heard that news and being consumed by the grief born of their separation, desired to abandon his life in that very fire; however, he was restrained with great effort by his ministers.'"
Vāsavadattā—
(To herself) I know, I know my noble husband’s compassion toward me.
*Yaugandharāyaṇa*: And then what happened?
*Brahmacārī*: Then the king, having embraced the ornaments remaining from her body after they had been consumed by fire, fell into a swoon.
*All*: Alas!
Vāsavadattā—
(To herself) May the noble Yaugandharāyaṇa now have his desire fulfilled.
Maid: Noble lady, this noble lady is indeed weeping.
Padmāvatī: She must be sympathetic.
[One must be compassionate.
Yaugandharāyaṇa: Indeed so, indeed so!
By nature my sister is compassionate.
Then, then.
(Brahmacārī)—Then, very gradually, he regained consciousness.
(Padmāvatī)—By good fortune, he survives!
"Having heard that he has fallen into a swoon, my heart feels as if it were empty.
(BhSv_1.12:54) [By good fortune he survives;
having heard that he has fallen into a swoon, my heart feels as if it were empty.]
Yaugandharāyaṇa: And then what happened?

Brahmacārī: Then that king, his body dusted with the soil from crawling upon the surface of the earth, suddenly rose up and lamented at great length, crying out, "Alas, Vāsavadattā! Alas, daughter of the King of Avanti! Alas, my beloved! Alas, my dear pupil!"
What need is there for more?
At this time, there are no such ruddy geese, nor indeed any others, who are separated from their beloved mates.
Blessed is that woman whom her husband knows [to be so dear] in such a way; for through her love for her husband, she remains unburned even though she has been consumed by fire.
Yaugandharāyaṇa: Now, sir, there is no minister who has made an effort to console him.
Brahmacārī: There is a minister named Rumaṇvat who is making a firm effort to console his honor.
For he...

Equal in his lack of food, with a face emaciated by constant weeping, and bearing upon his body a refinement that shares the king’s suffering, the subordinate king serves the sovereign with efforts day or night; yet if the king should suddenly give up his life, the subordinate king also perishes.
Vāsavadattā—
(To herself) By good fortune, my noble husband is now well-settled.
*{Yaugandharāyaṇa:*— *{To himself:} Oh, how great a burden Rumaṇvat bears!
Why is that?}
For this burden is indeed accompanied by rest, whereas his [the king's] labor is incessant;
for everything depends upon him, O Lord of Men, upon whom the ruler himself depends.
[Aloud] Oh, now that king has been established in the religious life (*brahmacārī*). Therefore, I do not know now whether he laughed here with her,
conversed here with her, stayed the night here with her, or [did other things] here with her.
Thinking, "He has gone to bed with her while he was angry," the ministers seized the king as he was thus lamenting from that village with great effort and departed.
Once the king had left, that village became unpleasant, like the sky when the moon has departed and the stars have vanished.
Then I too departed as an ascetic woman—
[thinking]: "He is indeed a king worthy of the name Guṇavant, since he is praised in this way even by this newcomer."
Maid: Noble lady, will another woman indeed fall into his hands?
Padmāvatī: [She speaks.]
[This was] deliberated by me only with my own heart.
The Brahmachari said: "I take leave of you both."
"Let us go for now. "Both of you, go for the accomplishment of your purpose. "So be it," [said the brahmacārī].
*Yaugandharāyaṇa* has exited.
*Yaugandharāyaṇa*: "Very well; having been permitted by her ladyship, I too wish to depart.
*Chamberlain*: "It is said that he wishes to depart, having been permitted by her ladyship."
Padmāvatī: My noble brother’s sister will long for him in his absence.
Yaugandharāyaṇa: Having fallen into the hands of virtuous people, she shall not long for him.
(Looking at the chamberlain) We shall depart for now. (The Chamberlain) May you go, sir,
to see [her] again.
*Yaugandharāyaṇa*: So be it.
*(Exit)* *Chamberlain*: It is now time to enter the inner apartments.
Padmāvatī: Noble lady, I pay you homage.
Ascetic: Daughter, may you obtain a husband equal to yourself.
"Once born, may you obtain a husband worthy of yourself.
Vāsavadattā: "Noble lady, I first pay my respects to you."
Ascetic: May you too, in no long time, be reunited with your husband.
Vāsavadattā: I am favored.
[“I am favored.
Chamberlain: “Therefore, please come this way;
this way, lady.”
For now,
the birds have returned to their nests, the sages have descended into the waters, the blazing fire shines forth, and smoke drifts through the hermitage grove;
the sun, having fallen from afar with its rays withdrawn, turns its chariot and slowly enters the peak of the western mountain.
[All exit. End of the First Act. Then enters a maidservant.
Maidservant: Kuñjarike, Kuñjarike! Where, where is the noble lady Padmāvatī?
"What do you say? That the noble lady is playing with a ball near the Mādhavī-creeper bower?
[Approaching] "I shall go up to the noble lady.

[Walking about and looking] "Ah! Here is the noble lady, her face beautiful even in exhaustion, with her ear-ornaments pushed back and drops of perspiration appearing on her left cheek from her play with the ball."
Kīḷandī is coming this very way;
I shall approach her. (Kuñjarike, Kuñjarike, where, where is the princess Padmāvatī?)
"What do you say? That this young lady is playing with a ball beside the Mādhavī-creeper bower?
Well then, I shall approach the young lady.

Ah! Here comes the young lady, playing with a ball, her face appearing beautiful even in exhaustion, adorned with artificially fashioned ear-ornaments and speckled with drops of perspiration born of her exertion.
"I shall go to meet her.
[She exits.
Interlude.
Then enters Padmāvatī, playing with a ball, accompanied by her attendants and Vāsavadattā.
Vāsavadattā: Friend, here is your ball!
Padmāvatī: Noble lady, let it be so for now.
Vāsavadattā: Friend, having played with the ball for too long, your hands have become so swollen that they seem almost like those of another person.
[“O friend! Having played with the ball for so long, your hands have become as if belonging to another, so red with passion.
*Slave Girl:* Let the young mistress play, let her play for now!
Let this time, delightful for the sport of maidenhood, first be brought to an end.
"Let the princess play, let her play! Let this period of time, so delightful in its maidenhood, be brought to an end.
Padmāvatī: "Noble lady, why do you now look at me as if to mock me?"
"Noble lady, why do you now look at me as if to mock me?
Vāsavadattā: "No, no!
My friend, today she looks even more beautiful."
"Is it not as if I am seeing your beautiful face today?
No, no! Friend, it shines even more today; I see your beautiful face as if it were closer."
Padmāvatī: Go away! Do not mock me now! [Go away! Do not mock me now!]
Vāsavadattā: Here I am; silent, I shall remain silent, O bride of Mahāsena.
Padmāvatī: Who is this named Mahāsena?
[“Who is this person named Mahāsena?
Vāsavadattā: There is a king of Ujjayinī named Pradyota;
his name is Mahāsena, derived from the measure of his army.
"There is a king in Ujjayinī named Pradyota;
his name, derived from the extent of his army, is Mahāsena.
The maidservant said: "The princess does not wish for a connection with that king."
"The princess does not wish for a union with that king.
Vāsavadattā: "Then with whom indeed does she now desire it?"
Maid:
There is a prince named Udayana; the young lady desires his virtues.
The princess longs for his virtues.
Vāsavadattā—
(to herself)— she longs for my noble husband as her lord.
[Aloud: For what reason does she desire the noble son as her husband?
For what reason?
Maid:
"He is compassionate. Vāsavadattā:—
"I know, I know;
even this person has gone mad in this way.
[I know, I know.]
[This person, too, has been driven thus to madness. Maid: Noble lady, if that king were ugly—
Vāsavadattā: No, no;
he is indeed handsome.
Padmāvatī: Noble lady, how do you know?
Vāsavadattā:
[To herself] Because of my partiality for the noble lord, I have transgressed the public consensus.
What shall I do now? Very well, it is seen.
[Aloud] Oh, this is what the people of Ujjayinī are saying!
Out of partiality for my noble husband, I have transgressed proper conduct;
what shall I do now?
"Let it be; I have seen it.
Indeed, this is what the people of Ujjayinī are saying.
Padmāvatī: "It is as you say."
Indeed, this is not difficult to find in Ujjayinī;
for that which is called "good fortune," which delights the hearts of all people, is certainly possible here.
[It is appropriate. Indeed, this is not difficult to find in Ujjayinī.
Indeed, that which is called "good fortune" is truly delightful to the minds of all people.
[Then enters the Nurse.
Nurse: Victory to the Princess!
"O noble lady, you have been given away.
(Victory to the noble lady!
Noble lady, you have been given away.)
Vāsavadattā: Noble lady, for whom?
Nurse: For Prince Udāyana.
*Vāsavadattā*: Is that King Udayana, the Prince, well? [Then:
Is that King well?
Nurse:
He has arrived in good health, and his young lady has been received by him.
And his daughter was accepted as a bride.
Vāsavadattā: This is a great calamity!
Nurse— What is the emergency here? Vāsavadattā— Nothing at all.
"It is not at all so; for even after having been thus tormented, one becomes indifferent.

*Nurse*: Noble lady, those who are devoted to the sacred scriptures, whose mental disturbances are easily overcome, possess the heart of a great man.
*Vāsavadattā*: Noble lady, she was chosen by him herself.
[Noble Lady, she was chosen by him herself.
Nurse: No, no!
When he came here for another purpose, the Great King saw her noble birth, discernment, and beauty, and gave her to him of his own accord.
[“No, no! Having seen his noble lineage, learning, age, and appearance, the Great King gave her to me of his own accord when he arrived here for another purpose.
Vāsavadattā—(to herself)—So it is! (BhSv_2:60)
Now the noble son is innocent here.
(Another enters.)
Maid: Hurry, hurry, mistress! Our lady says that today is indeed an auspicious constellation;
the festive rites must be performed this very day.
"Hurry, hurry, noble lady! Today indeed is an auspicious constellation; today alone must the festive rites be performed—so says our mistress."
Vāsavadattā— (to herself): The more he hastens, the more he makes my heart blind with longing.
Nurse: Come, come, my lady!
(All exit.)
The Second Act.
Now begins the Third Act.
Then enters Vāsavadattā, reflecting.

Vāsavadattā: Having left Padmāvatī behind in the inner courtyard, crowded with the festivities of the wedding, I have come here to this pleasure grove so that I may now dispel my sorrow brought about by misfortune. (Walking about) Oh, what a calamity!
Even my noble husband has become someone belonging to another!
I shall sit down.
{Having sat down} Blessed indeed is the female ruddy goose who does not live when separated from her mate.
Indeed, I do not abandon my life-breaths;
it is with this hope, "I shall see my noble lord," that I, unfortunate as I am, continue to live.
Amidst the bustle of the wedding festivities, I abandoned Padmāvatī in the inner apartment's quadrangle and have come here to the pleasure grove.
Now, while I am dispelling this suffering brought about by my fate—
alas, what a calamity!
Even my noble husband has indeed become someone belonging to another.
I shall sit down for a while.
Blessed indeed is the female ruddy goose who does not live when separated from her mate;
as for me, I certainly do not intend to give up my life.
"I live, unfortunate as I am, with this longing: 'May I see my noble son.
[Then enters a maidservant carrying flowers.
Maidservant: Where indeed has the noble lady Āvantikā gone?
{Walking around and looking about} Oh! Here she is, her heart empty with anxiety, wearing an unadorned yet auspicious dress like the moonlight obscured by mist, seated upon a slab of emerald.
I shall approach her.
{Approaching} Noble lady of Avanti, who am I that I should seek you out?
"Where indeed has the noble lady from Avantī gone? Alas!
Her heart is empty with anxiety; like a crescent moon obscured by mist, she sits upon this slab of priyaṅgu stone, wearing her simple yet auspicious attire.
I shall now approach her."
"Noble lady of Avanti, what is the reason that I am searching for you? Vāsavadattā:
"For what purpose?"
Maid:
Our mistress says, "Since you are born of a noble family, affectionate, and skillful, you must first enter this theater pavilion."
"Let the noble lady weave this garland of curiosities first.
Vāsavadattā: "To whom, pray, should it be woven?"
Maid: For our mistress' daughter.
Vāsavadattā: [For our mistress' daughter. Vāsavadattā:—
"This too was something that ought to have been done by me;
alas, the Lord is indeed merciless!
[This too was something that ought to have been done by me.]
"Alas, the lords are indeed merciless!
*Maidservant:* "Noble lady, do not worry now;
this son-in-law is being bathed on the jeweled floor."
"Venerable lady, please hide yourself quickly! Do not think of anything else now; this son-in-law is bathing on the jeweled floor."
"Let the noble lady weave it quickly.
Vāsavadattā—
(to herself)— I am unable to think of anything else.

The King:

Yaugandharāyaṇa: We are the followers of our master’s fortunes.
Padmāvatī: Oh, this is indeed my noble lady!

The King: Friend Yaugandharāyaṇa, what was the thought that led you to the removal of the Queen?

King: "Rumaṇvat has known this as well.

King: Ah, Rumaṇvat is indeed treacherous!

King: No, no!
